title: Native game engines
author: Critical_Hunter_6924
selftext: Was scrolling through this sub to realise that most people here are making web games. I was wondering if there are any fellow gamedevs willing to share their tips and experience using native game engines like unity or godot. What's the obsession with three.js, to me it seems like a bottleneck that could easily be avoided.

comments.author: JjyKs
comments.body:
Biggest problem with Unity/Godot/Unreal etc is that they're designed editor first. MCPs exist, but the LLM often lacks the context it needs. 

I've personally worked around that by making the scene really simple, single script that just starts building the scene from the code and handle everything with that. However I've now moved to custom C++ engine and that really seems to help Opus to figure stuff out. No outdated memories and no black boxes that need documentation to understand.

comments.author: discattho
comments.body: Web based games are just a smaller lift and current models are just better at it. Engines like UE5 and godot are massive code bases which are not so simple as prompting a game into existence. The user still needs to know a significant amount of the engine or game development to make anything worth noting.

comments.author: Slackluster
comments.body:
Try LittleJS Engine! It is a free and open source engine with a comprehensive feature set. What really sets it apart is how small and fast it is. No code bloat in the engine makes it very easy for AI to work with.

I made a special repo for developing games with AI: [https://github.com/KilledByAPixel/LittleJS-AI](https://github.com/KilledByAPixel/LittleJS-AI)

Here are 50+ games I made with it (also opensource): [https://killedbyapixel.github.io/LittleJSArcade/](https://killedbyapixel.github.io/LittleJSArcade/)

replies.author: Shadowlance23
replies.body:
The big one for me is that it interacts with the scene tree in the UI so I can get it to create nodes and scenes. It doesn't just dump everything into code files (well, it does, but I tell it to move stuff into nodes).

Basically if you can edit it in the UI, the AI can work with it too. E.g. it can create tile sets and set up the neighbour flags.

This makes it significantly easier for me when I'm doing manual work because it means all the parameters and set up stuff is easily accessible. It also means any work I do in adding nodes is seamlessly picked up by the AI.

I know all of this can be done programmatically, but it makes the code much easier to work with. It also means the AI can target a specific node or script file without needed to load the entire project into the context window.

I'm not hugely experienced with AI agents or Godot, so I don't know if this is the best way of doing it, but it works really well for me.

comments.author: PatchyWhiskers
comments.body: AI is simply better at Javascript due to more training data, and Unity and Godot have lots and lots of settings files that are opaque to LLMs and designed to be used with a GUI.

comments.author: massivebacon
comments.body:
I’ve got my own “native” game engine (https://github.com/zinc-framework) that I started prior to AI that is totally code driven. Turns out with AI is has been really great to have because everything is addressable by AI. With AI the main thing you want is that an AI can easily (and deterministically) touch all parts of the game, and ideally has a nice feedback cycle with the engine.

I recently incorporated a cross-platform screenshot solution as well for exactly this reason, so an AI can try something, take a screenshot, then look at the screenshot. I also have it use a command line image diffing tool (https://github.com/dmtrKovalenko/odiff) to compare expected results with whatever it was operating on before.

comments.author: Laicbeias
comments.body:
I used unity for 9 years. You cant really ai gen that stuff. With js you get a text based surface an ai can deal with. In unity you build settings and editors around you behaviours.

And.. i mean its the reality of gamedev, the complexer the system the more surface it has. The number of costum vars across materials, shaders, behaviours is astronomical. Like im backend dev for a larger 
soccer company, and the db surface of all fields we have. Is basically 3-4 gameobjects.

With AI this isnt fully solved, they can generate those 1 day demo
s or certain genres quickly. But those that you can generate quickly will become saturated, since they are pulled out from the training data.

That said iterating on unity games is hell. Step into play mode takes too long. They dropped billions on crap and never got their editor fixed. Their editor is the og slop. So yeah the complexity doesnt go away and the main goals for productivity in game dev is iteration speed. And unity falls flat on its face there. AI on scale will bleed you dry before, and gamedev needs taste now more than ever

replies.author: Laicbeias
replies.body:
Then.. where do you adjust and iterate the settings for basically anything? Because a game is 80% entangled data. Each shader settings. Each unit settings. Each door settings. Each behaviour settings. Each animation settings. Each texture settings. Each menu settings. Each light. Each i think you get what i mean. Who configures the game to be coherent in the eyes of a human.

The alternative is just boilerplate from known game templates. Asset flip 3.0. If we think that games will work like asset flipping a website they wont. It will be filtered out by players. Ai has lowered the floor and heightend the ceiling, especially for game dev
